syllabus.clause: Miri interprets MIR and detects provenance, aliasing and validity violations, data races and weak-memory behaviours (Jung et al., POPL 2026).
Its limits: speed, FFI, and only the paths actually executed.

Miri's own README states the identical limitation directly, in its own words: Miri can tell you whether one particular way of interacting with your code causes undefined behavior in one particular execution, among the many an unexplored branch could have taken. The Unstable Book's own AddressSanitizer docs name a different, complementary tool with its own different real reach. Does this topic's own small interpreter model exactly the limitation both sources describe?

syllabus.clause: Run cargo +nightly miri test in CI.
The -Zsanitizer flag is still nightly-only, though the Tier 2 x86_64-unknown-linux-gnuasan target lets AddressSanitizer run from a stable compiler;
AddressSanitizer/LeakSanitizer are close to stabilization, while MemorySanitizer/ThreadSanitizer need an instrumented std.

items.item: Miri is an Undefined Behavior detection tool for Rust, able to run binaries and test suites of cargo projects and detect unsafe code that fails to uphold its safety requirements

items.item: AddressSanitizer is a memory error detector that can detect out-of-bound accesses to heap, stack and globals, use after free and use after scope
AddressSanitizer works with non-instrumented code although it will impede its ability to detect some bugs, and is not expected to produce false positive reports

items.item: Miri's own broader real detection list (data races, weak-memory effects, the experimental Stacked Borrows and Tree Borrows aliasing checks) is named and explained in post-notes rather than measured here, since this topic's own interpreter models only the one, simplest case (an out-of-bounds access) that is easiest to check safely and deterministically without a real Miri session.

The -Zsanitizer flag's own current, real state (nightly-only overall, but the Tier 2 x86_64-unknown-linux-gnuasan target allowing a stable AddressSanitizer build) is explained in post-notes rather than measured, since actually building with a sanitizer is a real toolchain/target configuration this sandboxed container's own pinned stable toolchain cannot exercise.

A sanitizer's own real reach (instrumenting compiled machine code, catching errors at native speed, reaching real FFI and I/O) is explained in post-notes by direct contrast with Miri's own platform-independent interpreter, which is the genuinely different tool/reach the syllabus's own clause on sanitizers is naming.

All of this topic's own measured claims run entirely on plain in-memory Rust values, a plain fixed-size struct array, and a plain usize counter, with no file, network, root access, or actual nightly Miri session; 'the interpreter', 'the branch', and 'the checker' are all real, deterministic Rust values and functions, continuing this domain's own established pattern.
